title: ARTEX: an AI pentest framework, its copies, and what defenders should do
content_md: Research note, 17 November 2026. Static analysis only. I did not run any cloned code or binary, and I did not scan or probe any host. ARTEX is an open-source AI penetration-testing framework. Within about six weeks of its last release it showed up by name in an FBI flash advisory, a Microsoft supply-chain attribution, a CrowdStrike espionage campaign, and a Korean bank breach investigation. The original repository is gone. Hundreds of copies remain, plus thousands of forks. One Docker image was backdoored. The source tree still contains a comment saying the authorization guard was removed. I rebuilt the picture from primary sources: the threat-intel record, the surviving git history, the copies and forks, the binaries people publish, and the frameworks it gets compared to. This note covers six things: What is on GitHub. Which copies are original, and which are faithful. Whether any are malicious. What differs between them. How ARTEX works, and whether it does anything a plain agent harness does not. What defenders should do. The short version: the model and the exploit are not the interesting part. The packaging is. ARTEX wraps an agent loop, a task graph, and a web console into one binary, and that turns a general model into something a low-skill operator can point at a target. 1.
